rationale: Start with a broad mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to span the mixture and reveal overall retention, elution window, and any missing late compounds. This gives a balanced first map of selectivity versus run time for the 10-component mixture.

All 10 compounds are already baseline resolved with substantial margin, so the main opportunity is to reduce the time penalty. Keeping selectivity fixed and shortening the gradient should compress the run while checking whether the closest cluster around peaks 5 to 7 remains adequately resolved.

The 10-minute gradient is fast but over-compressed the central cluster, with peaks 6 and 7 dropping to R = 0.62. A small increase in gradient time should recover resolution around that cluster while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve a strong CRF.

Resolution improved strongly from 10 to 12 minutes, but the same pair is still just under baseline at R = 1.01. Extending slightly to 14 minutes should test whether that pair crosses into comfortable resolution while likely keeping the time penalty at zero.

The trend suggests the limiting pair continues to open as gradient time increases, and at 14 minutes it is only slightly below 1.5. Testing 16 minutes should determine whether full baseline resolution is reached and whether that yields the maximum attainable CRF despite a modest time penalty.

The optimum in gradient time appears to sit near 14 minutes, so the remaining lever is selectivity rather than longer runtime. A modest temperature decrease may selectively open the critical 6/7 pair enough to reach full resolution at the same 14-minute gradient without incurring the time penalty seen at 16 minutes.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing a different central pair, so the better direction is to test a modest increase from the current optimum. At fixed 14-minute gradient, 45 C may improve the critical cluster enough to exceed the 40 C result without adding time penalty.

Temperature changes worsened the central selectivity, so return to 40 C and probe solvent-program shape instead. Lowering phi0 while keeping phi1 and tG fixed should increase early gradient occupancy and may spread the crowded mid-eluting cluster enough to improve the limiting pair without increasing runtime much.

Changing phi0 downward did not help, so test the opposite direction while keeping the apparent time optimum and best temperature fixed. A slightly higher phi0 may weaken retention differences among the earliest compounds but can reshape the gradient enough to open the crowded middle pair around peaks 6 and 7.

Phi0 shifts around the 14-minute optimum only changed the critical pair slightly, so now test a slightly less aggressive final organic strength to alter late-gradient selectivity while preserving the same overall slope region. This may decompress the central cluster enough to push the 6/7 pair over baseline without needing the longer 16-minute run.

You already achieved the maximum CRF, so any further run is only exploratory; the safest nearby perturbation is a small reduction in phi1 from the optimum. This tests whether the score plateau extends to slightly weaker final strength while staying close to the proven best selectivity and runtime region.

The optimum appears sensitive mainly to phi1, with 0.85 outperforming 0.90 and 0.80, so keep phi1 at 0.85 and probe a small phi0 increase around that best region. This checks whether a slightly steeper effective early gradient can retain full resolution while trimming retention relative to the 0.10/0.85 method.

You already have a CRF plateau at 1.000 around phi1 = 0.85, and increasing phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 retained full resolution while shortening the run. Testing phi0 = 0.20 explores whether that plateau extends to an even faster variant with baseline separation still preserved.

The best region is now centered at phi1 = 0.85 and phi0 = 0.10-0.15, with 14 minutes giving full resolution. Shortening tG to 12 minutes at the stronger-performing 0.15/0.85 composition tests whether the same selectivity gain from phi1 can preserve baseline separation in a faster run.

The CRF maximum spans phi0 = 0.10-0.15 at phi1 = 0.85, while phi0 = 0.20 starts to lose the critical separation. Testing phi0 = 0.05 completes the local map around the optimum and checks whether a lower starting strength can maintain full resolution at the same zero-penalty runtime.

The 1.000-CRF plateau is best centered at phi1 = 0.85, and phi0 = 0.15 gave the shorter of the two perfect runs. Testing phi1 = 0.80 at phi0 = 0.15 checks whether this nearby composition also stays on the maximum plateau or falls into the longer-runtime behavior seen at 0.10/0.80.

The local optimum is already found, so use remaining runs to map nearby boundaries of the CRF plateau. Since phi0 = 0.20 was too high at phi1 = 0.85, testing the compensating stronger endpoint phi1 = 0.90 shows whether that loss was due to phi0 alone or the phi0/phi1 combination.

With the maximum CRF already achieved, a useful remaining check is how robust the phi1 = 0.85 optimum is to a longer gradient. This tests whether the perfect score at 0.10/0.85/14 is a sharp runtime optimum or part of a broader fully resolved plateau.

You have already identified the best-performing composition family, so this final local check separates composition effects from gradient-time effects. Running the other perfect composition at 16 minutes will show whether both 1.000 methods lose score similarly from added time or if one is intrinsically more robust.

The optimum is fully established at 40 C, but the temperature effect has only been mapped for phi1 = 0.90. Testing 35 C at the phi1 = 0.85 optimum family checks whether the improved solvent selectivity changes the thermal response enough to retain the 1.000 plateau or confirms that 40 C is the unique best temperature.

Temperature sensitivity clearly matters, but it has not been tested for the second 1.000-CRF composition. Checking 45 C at 0.15/0.85/14 completes the thermal map around the best region and confirms whether 40 C is robustly optimal there as well.

The best operating region is fully mapped, so the remaining value is defining the lower-phi1 edge of acceptable performance. Dropping phi1 one more step from 0.80 to 0.75 at the original optimum composition will show how sharply the time penalty grows on the weaker-endpoint side.

With only a few injections left and the optimum already reached, a useful final boundary point is the high-phi0/low-phi1 corner near the best region. This will define how quickly the 1.000 plateau collapses when both parameters move away from the optimum in the same direction.

Injection 23 unexpectedly showed the 1.000 plateau extends farther toward higher phi0 and lower phi1 than expected. A one-step increase to phi0 = 0.25 at the same phi1 = 0.80 tests the edge of that plateau while staying in the newly validated optimum family.

The last run showed phi0 = 0.25 is too aggressive at phi1 = 0.80 because the first pair collapsed near the dead-time region. Raising phi1 one step to 0.85 for the final injection tests whether that failure was specific to the low endpoint and helps define the upper phi0 boundary of the 1.000 plateau.
